question: A patient admitted with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is started on IV ceftriaxone. At 72 hours, blood and sputum cultures are negative. The patient has been afebrile for 48 hours, CRP is falling, and they are tolerating oral intake. What is the most appropriate AMSP-consistent action?

answers.text: Switch to oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and discharge with a total of 5 days antibiotic duration (IV + oral)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IDSA/ATS guidelines and AMSP principles support IV-to-oral switch once clinical stability criteria are met (afebrile ≥48 h, improving, tolerating oral intake). A total course of 5 days is sufficient for non-severe CAP — shorter courses reduce adverse effects and resistance selection.

answers.text: Continue IV ceftriaxone for a total of 10 days as per traditional pneumonia treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Traditional 10-day IV courses are no longer recommended for non-severe CAP. Prolonged IV therapy increases hospital stay, catheter-related complications, costs, and resistance selection pressure without improving clinical outcomes.

answers.text: Escalate to piperacillin–tazobactam because negative cultures suggest a resistant organism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Negative cultures are common in CAP (50–70% of cases) and do not indicate resistance. Escalation in a clinically improving patient contradicts AMSP de-escalation principles and exposes the patient to unnecessary broad-spectrum selection pressure.

answers.text: Continue IV antibiotics until fully asymptomatic to prevent relapse

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Clinical stability — not complete symptom resolution — is the threshold for step-down therapy. Waiting for full symptom resolution prolongs hospitalisation unnecessarily and is not supported by evidence for preventing CAP relapse.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the AMSP principles of de-escalation and IV-to-oral switch: when a patient meets clinical stability criteria, step down to oral therapy and aim for the shortest effective total course.
Excellent. IV-to-oral switch and shortened antibiotic courses are core AMSP strategies that reduce harm without compromising patient outcomes.
